questions.q: A new TypeScript project imports node:fs/promises and tsc says Cannot find name 'node:fs/promises'. Where do the missing types come from?
questions.explain: Node.js ships no TypeScript types. The DefinitelyTyped project publishes them as @types/node: .d.ts files that only describe the API. You install it and list "node" in the types field of tsconfig.json.
options: From Node.js itself: upgrading Node.js adds them
From the @types/node package, which describes Node.js in declaration files
From tsx, which generates them when it runs

questions.q: Why is @types/node installed with -D (as a development dependency)?
questions.explain: Declaration files contain no runnable code. The compiler reads them; the running server never does. So they belong with the other build tools in devDependencies.
options: Because it is only allowed in development, never in production builds
Because types are only used while writing and checking code; nothing in them runs
Because it is large and -D compresses it
Because -D makes tsc load it automatically without tsconfig.json

questions.q: Your servers run Node.js 24, but the project installed the newest @types/node, which describes a later Node.js. What can go wrong?
questions.explain: The types only describe an API; they do not check which Node.js will run the code. If they describe a newer release, you can call something your runtime lacks and get is not a function in production. Pin @types/node to the Node.js major version you deploy.
options: Nothing: newer types are always backwards compatible
tsc refuses to run until the versions match
Code can use a function that type-checks but does not exist in Node.js 24, and it crashes at runtime

questions.q: With @types/node and strict on, what is the type of process.env["TOKEN_SECRET"]?
questions.explain: Environment variables are always text, and any of them can be missing. That is exactly what string | undefined says, so the compiler makes you handle the missing case.

questions.q: A developer adds interface ProcessEnv { TOKEN_SECRET: string } inside declare global { namespace NodeJS { … } }. What does that change?
questions.explain: Declaration merging is a promise to the compiler that nothing verifies. When the server starts without the variable, code that trusted the type crashes, often far from startup. Parse the environment in code instead.
options: Node.js now refuses to start when TOKEN_SECRET is missing
tsx checks the variable when the program starts
Only the type: process.env.TOKEN_SECRET is typed string, but it can still be undefined at runtime
It sets a default value of ""

questions.q: Why does loadConfig(env: Env) take the environment as a parameter instead of reading process.env inside?
questions.explain: A function whose inputs are all parameters is easy to test: pass { PORT: "-1" } and check the error. The server passes process.env, which fits the Env type.
options: Because process.env cannot be read inside a function
So tests can pass a plain object, and the function has no hidden input
So TypeScript can infer the type of every variable

questions.q: Why does the lesson's loadConfig collect every problem before throwing, instead of throwing at the first one?
questions.explain: A deployment with three wrong settings should take one fix, not three restarts. The server still refuses to start; it just says everything that is wrong.
options: Throwing is slow, so it is done only once
Because ConfigError can only be created once
So the person deploying sees every wrong setting at once, instead of fixing one per restart
So the server can start anyway with the valid settings

questions.q: At startup you want to log the configuration the server is using. What should the log line contain for tokenSecret?
questions.explain: Logs are copied, shipped to other services and read by many people. A secret in a log is a leaked secret; even part of one helps an attacker. base64 is an encoding, not protection. Log that it is set and how long it is.
options: The whole secret, so operators can check it
The first 8 characters of the secret
Something about the secret that is safe, like its length, but never its value

questions.q: What is the type of data in const data = await readFile("prices.json");?
questions.explain: readFile has overloads. Without an encoding it returns the raw bytes as a Buffer; with "utf8" it returns a string. The compiler picks the return type from the arguments.
options: any, because the file could contain anything

questions.q: readTextIfExists returns undefined when the error code is ENOENT, and throws every other error again. Why not return undefined for every error?
questions.explain: Only "the file does not exist" is an expected, harmless case. EACCES or EISDIR mean something is broken; hiding them turns a loud failure into silent data loss.
options: Because other errors have no code property
Because a permission or disk error would then look like "no file yet", and the program would start over with empty data
Because re-throwing is required by TypeScript
Because ENOENT is the only error readFile can throw

questions.q: Why does the lesson write const data: unknown = JSON.parse(text);?
questions.explain: With any, data.quantity.toFixed() compiles whatever the file contains. Storing the result as unknown means nothing can touch it until a type guard proves its shape.
options: JSON.parse returns any, which turns type checking off; unknown forces a check before use

questions.q: Inside a server's request handler, why is req.url typed string | undefined?
questions.explain: For a server, Node.js always fills in the method and URL. But IncomingMessage also represents the response an HTTP client receives, which has neither. A fallback like req.url ?? "/" handles the type honestly.
options: Because clients may send requests without a URL
Because the same IncomingMessage type is used for client responses, where there is no URL
Because the URL is only available after the body has been read
It is a mistake in @types/node that you should fix with !

questions.q: After server.listen(0), what can server.address() return, according to its type?
questions.explain: That is why the lesson checks address === null || typeof address === "string" before reading address.port. Writing as AddressInfo would silently ignore two real cases.
options: An AddressInfo, a string (a Unix socket path), or null (not listening yet)

questions.q: A request arrives with the Idempotency-Key header twice, with the values t-1 and t-2. What does req.headers["idempotency-key"] give, and how do you insist on exactly one value?
questions.explain: For most headers Node.js joins repeated values with a comma, so req.headers cannot show that there were two. req.headersDistinct keeps each value separately. For a security-relevant header, two values are suspicious, and "missing" (a 400) is the safe answer.
options: "t-1, t-2", joined into one string; read req.headersDistinct and accept only a list of length 1

questions.q: Why does sendJson set content-length with Buffer.byteLength(text) instead of text.length?
questions.explain: "₦" has length 1 but is 3 bytes. A too-small content-length makes the client cut the body off; a too-large one makes it wait for bytes that never come.
options: Because the header counts bytes, and characters like ₦ take more than one byte in UTF-8
Because text.length includes the quotes of the JSON

questions.q: You write a function that hashes bytes. Which parameter type makes it work with both Buffers and the output of TextEncoder?
questions.explain: Buffer is a subclass of Uint8Array, so a Buffer fits a Uint8Array parameter. A plain Uint8Array does not fit a Buffer parameter, because it lacks methods such as toString("hex").

questions.q: A stage is declared as async function* toLines(chunks: AsyncIterable<string>) and receives a file stream opened without an encoding. What happens?
questions.explain: Types are erased at runtime, and a stream's chunks are any, so nothing checks the annotation. It is a claim you must make true at the source, for example with { encoding: "utf8" }.
options: tsc reports that a stream of buffers is not an iterable of strings
It compiles, because stream chunks are typed any, and at runtime it receives Buffers
Node.js converts the chunks to strings automatically because of the annotation
It throws a TypeError on the first chunk

questions.q: A report reads a file in small chunks and decodes each chunk with chunk.toString(). Some customer names come out with � in them. What is the fix?
questions.explain: A multi-byte character can be cut between two chunks, and decoding each half alone produces replacement characters. The stream's own decoder carries the unfinished bytes over to the next chunk. Bigger chunks only make the bug rarer.
options: Use bigger chunks, so it happens less often
Let the stream decode (encoding: "utf8"), which keeps a character that is split across chunks together

questions.q: With new EventEmitter<ShopEvents>() from @types/node, which mistake does tsc report?
questions.explain: For names in the map, arguments are checked. Names outside the map are allowed on purpose and get any[], so a typo compiles and the emit goes nowhere. A small wrapper whose methods take keyof Events closes that gap.
options: Both a misspelt event name and a wrong payload
A wrong payload for a known event, but not a misspelt event name
A misspelt event name, but not a wrong payload
Neither: the type parameter is only documentation

questions.q: You call spawn(cmd, args, { stdio: ["ignore", "inherit", "inherit"] }). What is the type of child.stdout?
questions.explain: @types/node reads your stdio option. With "inherit", the child writes straight to your terminal and there is no stream to read, so the type is null. With "pipe" it is a Readable.

questions.q: A supervisor sends SIGTERM to a worker and later sees exit code 0 and signal null. What does that tell you?
questions.explain: A process killed by a signal reports code: null and the signal's name. Code 0 with no signal means the worker's SIGTERM handler ran and the process ended normally: a graceful shutdown.
options: The worker was killed by the signal before it could react
The worker handled the signal, finished its work and exited on its own

questions.q: Your server runs with tsx src/server.ts in production. A pull request adds a type error. What stops it from being deployed?
questions.explain: tsx and Node.js 24 strip types without checking them. Only tsc checks. Make tsc --noEmit a required step in CI.
options: tsx refuses to run files with type errors
Node.js checks types when it loads the file
Nothing, unless CI runs tsc --noEmit and blocks the merge

questions.q: You run node src/status.ts with Node.js 24, and the file declares an enum. What happens, and which tsconfig option warns you earlier?
questions.explain: Node.js only deletes type syntax. An enum or a parameter property produces JavaScript, so it cannot simply be deleted, and Node.js refuses the file. erasableSyntaxOnly makes tsc reject that syntax up front.
options: It runs fine; Node.js compiles enums
Node.js throws ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX; erasableSyntaxOnly makes tsc report it while you write
Node.js ignores the enum and every use becomes undefined; strict reports it
Node.js prints a warning and continues; noEmit reports it

questions.q: The deployment sets PORT to an empty string. What does this print?
questions.explain: ?? only replaces null and undefined. An empty string is kept, and Number("") is 0, a valid-looking integer. That is why the lesson checks the raw text with a regular expression before converting.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Number is forgiving: it accepts decimals, signs, surrounding spaces and turns "" into 0. None of those is a valid port. The regular expression only accepts 1 to 5 digits and nothing else.
options:
[ NaN, NaN, NaN, NaN ]
[ false, false, false, false ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: length counts UTF-16 code units: 4. In UTF-8, ₦ takes 3 bytes and each digit 1, so the byte length is 6.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: TextEncoder returns a plain Uint8Array. Its toString joins the byte values with commas. It has no encoding argument; that is a Buffer feature.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A missing file rejects with an error whose code is "ENOENT". The guard proves that the caught value is an Error with a string code, so reading error.code type-checks.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first is an Error without a code. The third has a code but is a plain object, not an Error. Only the second passes both checks.

questions.q: This helper reads a headersDistinct-style object, where every header maps to a list of values. What does it print?
questions.explain: Two values are refused, a single value is returned, and a missing header is undefined. For a header that must have exactly one value, two values count as "not given".

questions.q: The config object is frozen. What does this print?
questions.explain: The annotation { port: number } drops readonly, so the assignment compiles. At runtime the object is frozen, and in a module (always strict mode) writing to a frozen property throws a TypeError. Keep readonly in the type so the compiler catches it first.
options: Cannot assign to read only property 'port' of object '#<Object>'

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The misspelt name compiles, because @types/node allows names outside the map. emit returns false when no listener exists for the event, so the first line is false and no receipt is printed.
options:
receipt for 1001
true
receipt for 1002
true

questions.q: In what order are the lines printed?
questions.explain: emit calls every listener synchronously, in the order they were added, before it returns. Types do not change that behaviour.
options:
before emit
after emit
listener: order 7

before emit
listener: order 7
after emit

listener: order 7
before emit
after emit

questions.q: This is the lesson's toLines stage, fed three chunks. What does it print?
questions.explain: Chunk boundaries do not match line boundaries. rest keeps the unfinished end of the text until the next chunk arrives, and the last line, which has no final newline, is yielded after the loop.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A child that exits with a non-zero code makes the promise reject. The error carries the exit code in code. The guard "code" in error is needed because the catch variable is unknown.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: parseEnv understands .env syntax, including quotes, but every value is still a string. Turning "8080" into a checked number is the config loader's job.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: includes compares exactly, so capitals and abbreviations are refused. The as readonly string[] widens the array so includes accepts any string; the guard's return type then narrows the value.
options:
production true
Production true
prod true

production true
Production true
prod false

production true
Production false
prod false

production false
Production false
prod false

questions.q: Write parsePort(raw: string | undefined): number. Missing means 3000. Otherwise the text must be 1 to 5 digits and at most 65535, or it throws Error("bad PORT: " + raw). The program prints the results for four inputs.
questions.explain: Check the text before converting it. Number("") is 0 and Number("80.5") is 80.5, and neither is a port. Only a missing value gets the default; an empty string is a mistake.

questions.q: Finish loadConfig so it collects every problem and throws one Error whose message is the problems joined with "; ". Rules: TOKEN_SECRET at least 32 characters ("TOKEN_SECRET too short"), NODE_ENV one of development, test, production, default development ("bad NODE_ENV").
questions.explain: Push each problem into a list and throw once at the end. The person fixing the deployment then sees both mistakes in one go.
questions.expected:
development
TOKEN_SECRET too short; bad NODE_ENV

questions.q: Write describeConfig(config) for the startup log. It returns port=PORT secret=[N chars] and must never contain the secret itself.
questions.explain: JSON.stringify(config) is the easy way to leak a secret into logs. Build the log line from the fields that are safe, and describe the secret without showing it.

questions.q: Write the guard isErrnoLike(error: unknown): error is Error & { code: string } and use it in loadOrDefault: when read throws an error with code ENOENT, return "[]"; re-throw anything else.
questions.explain: Only "no such file" has a safe default. A permission error must reach the caller, or the program would carry on as if the data were empty.

questions.q: Finish the tiny strict emitter: on adds a listener to the list for its name, and emit calls every listener for that name with the arguments and returns whether there was one. Its method signatures only accept names from Events.
questions.explain: The storage is a mapped type: for each event name, a list of listeners of exactly that event's shape, so no cast is needed. The public methods are what matter: name: K with K extends keyof Events refuses any name outside the map, and ...args: Events[K] ties the arguments to that name.

questions.q: Write the async generator stage toOrders(lines): split each line id;customer;amountKobo, skip lines that do not have three parts, and yield typed OrderLine objects. Then total the kobo.
questions.explain: Destructuring an array can give undefined for missing parts, and with the lesson's strict settings TypeScript knows it. Checking all three before yielding both skips the broken line and narrows the types to string.

questions.q: Write byteLength(text) without Buffer, using TextEncoder, so it works in the browser too. Print the character count and byte count of "₦45,000".
questions.explain: TextEncoder encodes to UTF-8, where ₦ takes 3 bytes. The number of bytes is what a content-length header or a size limit must use.

questions.q: server.address() can return an object with a port, a string, or null. Write portOf(address) that returns the port, or throws Error("not a TCP address") for the other two cases, without using as.
questions.explain: After ruling out null and strings, only AddressInfo is left, so TypeScript lets you read port. A cast would compile too, but it would return undefined for a socket path instead of failing clearly.
questions.expected:
41234
not a TCP address
not a TCP address
